This page goes with **Chapter 9, Harmonic Progression and Harmonic Function** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/HarmonicProgression.html). Read each section there first; the book is the reference
for the terms used here. It builds on [Chapter 7, Roman Numerals](roman-numerals.qmd) and [Chapter 8, Seventh Chords](seventh-chords.qmd).

This chapter is about chords in order, so most of the practice here is **listening**. The drills play each progression on the piano (or
show it, or both); the clips are the book's own, cut where the book cuts them. Every drill has **Settings**, and is also on the
[Theory Drills](theory-drills.qmd) page.

**Typing a progression:** the chords in order with spaces between them: `I vi IV V`. Case is the quality, as before. Type `b` or `♭`
before a numeral for ♭VII. With *Answer with: lead-sheet symbols*, type `C Am F G` (a small letter is minor here too).

## 9.1 The circle of fifths progression

Each chord's root is a fifth above the next one's (or a fourth below): **I IV vii° iii vi ii V I** in major, **i iv VII III VI ii° V i**
in minor, with only the notes of the key, so one fifth (IV to vii°) is diminished. The bass makes a **sequence**: a short idea repeated
at a lower pitch, which is why the progression sounds so inevitable.
[Read 9.1](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/CircleOfFifths.html) ·
[Open Music Theory: Diatonic Sequences](https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/diatonic-sequences/)

<div class="drill" data-ex="prog" data-settings="groups=circle&mode=major&most=2&answer=rn&show=both"></div>

## 9.2 Harmonic rhythm

**Harmonic rhythm** is how long each chord lasts: a chord a bar in "Fly Me to the Moon" and "I Will Survive", two chords a bar in the
Mozart and Wagner. It can change inside a song: in "Pompeii" it doubles, from four beats a chord to two.
[Read 9.2](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/HarmonicRhythm.html)

::: {.rn-quiz}
<figure><figcaption>Bastille, "Pompeii": listen for the chords changing twice as often</figcaption>
<iframe class="dr-yt" src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/F90Cw4l-8NY?start=71&end=87&rel=0" title="Pompeii" loading="lazy" allowfullscreen></iframe></figure>
:::

## 9.3 Shorter progressions from the circle

Pieces of the circle are everywhere, especially in jazz standards and pop: **ii–V–I**; **vi–ii–V–I** and its rotations **I–vi–ii–V** and
**ii–V–I–vi**; **iii–vi–ii–V**, often looped, and its rotation **ii–V–iii–vi**.
[Read 9.3](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/ShorterProgressionsFromTheCircleOfFifths.html)

## 9.4 Harmonic function

A chord's **function** is what it tends to do next. The book uses four:

| Function | Major | Minor | Tends to |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tonic** (ton.) | I | i | rest; can go anywhere |
| **Tonic prolongation** (ton. prol.) | iii, vi | III, VI | move on to a pre-dominant |
| **Pre-dominant** (pre-dom.) | IV, ii | iv, ii° | move on to a dominant |
| **Dominant** (dom.) | V, vii° | V, vii° | go to the tonic |

In minor, **VII** (the subtonic) has one job: it leads to III. Two exceptions: **IV** has tonic prolongation function when it goes
straight to I (the plagal cadence), and **I/5th** has dominant function when it goes to V. The deceptive cadence (V–vi) is the other
exception to the flowchart.
[Read 9.4](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/HarmonicFunction.html) ·
[Open Music Theory: Introduction to Harmony](https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/intro-to-harmony/)

Name the function of a chord (keys: t, r, p, d):

<div class="drill" data-ex="func" data-settings="mode=both&most=4&show=staff&clef=treble,bass"></div>

## 9.5 Exceptions created by sequences

When a progression breaks the flowchart, look for a sequence: a pattern of chords repeated a step or more lower or higher, which takes
the chords wherever the pattern goes. The book's examples are "Flashdance... What a Feeling" (the book's clip of it is no longer on
YouTube) and the verse of "Hotel California":
[Read 9.5](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/ExceptionsCreatedBySequences.html)

::: {.rn-quiz}
<figure><figcaption>Eagles, "Hotel California", the verse</figcaption>
<iframe class="dr-yt" src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/BciS5krYL80?start=0&end=26&rel=0" title="Hotel California" loading="lazy" allowfullscreen></iframe></figure>
:::

## 9.6 ♭VII in popular music

In rock and pop, **♭VII** (a major chord on the lowered 7th, B♭ in C major) is everywhere. It can come before tonic, pre-dominant or
dominant chords, so it can stand in for any function except tonic, and **♭VII–IV–I** is a common way to end a phrase.
[Read 9.6](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/SubtonicVIIinPopMusic.html) ·
[Open Music Theory: Modal Schemas](https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/modal-schemas/)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## 9.7 The best-seller progression

**I–V–vi–IV** is in so many hit songs that it has its own name, and its rotations **vi–IV–I–V** and **IV–I–V–vi** are just as common.
vi–IV–I–V can also be heard in the relative minor as **i–VI–III–VII**: which one you hear depends on which chord feels like home.
[Read 9.7](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/BestsellerProgression.html) ·
[Open Music Theory: Four-Chord Schemas](https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/4-chord-schemas/)

## 9.8 i–VII–VI–VII

**i–VII–VI–VII** (Am G F G) walks the bass down from the tonic, like the flamenco "Andalusian" progression (Am G F E) but turning back
up at the end. It also comes rotated as **VI–VII–i–VII**, or **VI–VII–i–i**. In the relative major it is vi–V–IV–V.
[Read 9.8](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/i-VII-VI-VII.html)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## 9.9 Everything together

Every progression in the chapter, major and minor, by ear and eye. Set **Questions** to 20 for a score.

## For teachers

- **Links with your settings:** open a drill's **Settings**, then **Copy a link with these settings**. Add `&lock=1` for a test, `&count=20` for a score.
- **Progressions drilled:** the circle of fifths in major and minor and its pieces (ii–V–I, vi–ii–V–I, I–vi–ii–V, ii–V–I–vi, iii–vi–ii–V,
  ii–V–iii–vi); I–V–I, i–V–i, I–ii–V–I, I–IV–V–I, i–iv–V–i, I–vi–IV–V and IV–V–I–vi; I–V–vi–IV and its two rotations, I–♭VII–IV–I,
  i–VII–VI–VII, VI–VII–i–VII and VI–VII–i–i.
- **Voicing:** the drills play root-position triads (bass root, close chord above), two a bar. They are for hearing the bass and the
  qualities, not for voice leading, which the book takes up later.
- **Function drill:** root-position diatonic triads only. VII in minor is left out (the book gives it no function of its own), and the two
  exceptions (IV–I, I/5th–V) need context, so they are taught in the text, not drilled.
- **Videos:** the clips use the book's YouTube links and start and end times; each title was checked against YouTube. "Flashdance... What a Feeling" is no longer available there, so it is left out.
- The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
:::
